utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to greet the parties and all our staff and extend my greeting to the gallery. We can resume asking the witness. I forgot to greet the witness too. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution, Witness DB. Mr. President, the Defence wishes to inform you that in the course of today's hearings, General Krstic will not be attending due to problems of health, which have been confirmed by the doctors yesterday afternoon in the Detention Unit, so that as far as the Defence is aware, there might be some surgery. General Krstic agrees to continue today's hearings in his absence, and during the afternoon the Defence will have his written waiver prepared so that we can continue our hearings without further problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are aware of this and we wish General Krstic recovery and we'll continue the trial since he has agreed. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Petrusic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, we stopped yesterday when we were discussing the 13th of July, that is, the establishment of the forward command post in the village of Krivace. You said that you don't remember what time of day it was when you noticed General Krstic's presence, so my question is: Can you tell us which officers of the Drina Corps were present at the forward command post at Krivace for as long as it existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). In the logistics section of this forward command post, I remember the presence of Lieutenant Colonel Hendryk Jevitski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the forward command post existed in Krivace and later in Godenje, were other officers of the Drina Corps or the Main Staff present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the forward command post in Krivace and later Godenje, General Mladic would occasionally come, but he didn't stay for long. I think that he came in all two or three times throughout the duration of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Krstic present at the forward command post throughout the duration of the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic was present more or less all the time at the forward command post in the village of Krivace and the village of Godenje. I remember that he would occasionally go to tour the units participating in the operation, but all this took place within a radius of several kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While touring the units was he in radio contact or in contact in any other way with the forward command post and with the units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time he was connected to the command radio network in such a way that one of the soldiers with a mobile device would accompany him as he moved, or General Krstic himself would call from the command post of one of the subordinate units, using their transmitters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. You say one of the soldiers with a mobile device would accompany him as he moved. Was that a constant accompanying person, like a bodyguard accompanying somebody everywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a soldier from the communications battalion who would, pursuant to General Krstic's orders, go with him carrying the mobile equipment along. So depending on General Krstic's assessment as to whether he would need him while he was touring or while he was temporarily absent, this soldier with the mobile device would go with him in the jeep or on foot, if that was how -- if he could walk at the time. So the soldier was not from his -- a bodyguard or security unit, but from the communications centre of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: According to your knowledge and experience, a man in the position of a General would be constantly accompanied by a soldier for communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic had his own security and escort, physical escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm speaking of communication. The mobile device, is this part of a General's equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not the practice in our conditions for a part of the communications equipment to always accompany the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, who would decide whether when leaving the forward command post the General needed to have a communication line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the decision would be made by General Krstic himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this communication line that he would take with him leaving the forward command post, with whom could he establish contact by means of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the reserve mobile transmitters that could only be used within the same radio network of the units participating in the Zepa operation. So when he would leave the forward command post to go to the area of responsibility or the command post of one of the units participating in the Zepa operation, in his absence from the forward command post, he could command only those units that were participating in the operation because with that device which the soldier was carrying, the soldier from the communications centre, General Krstic could command only the units that were involved in the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, on the transcript, is that really the correct English translation, that he could "command only" the units, or should it be "communicate only" with the units? It says here, "In his absence ... he could command only those units participating in the operation because with that device," and then later on it repeats that, that he could "command only the units." I'm wondering if you don't mean communicate, if the English translation shouldn't be "communicate"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, in his absence from the forward command post, could General Krstic, using this device, communicate only with units participating in the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a device with limited range and voice protection, and the key that we used to protect the speech was available only to units participating in the Zepa operation. To explain this technically, this means that using this device, he could communicate only with the units participating in the Zepa operation. According to its technical properties, it has a range of 8 to 12 kilometres, but because of the characteristics of electromagnetic waves, its range is considerably reduced in a mountainous and wooded terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, do you know -- no, let me withdraw that. Do you know what position General Krstic held in the command of the Drina Corps on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that General Krstic was Chief of Staff of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to when General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this is an important question, but in my preparations for my testimony here, I read the order of the president of the Republika Srpska dated the 13th of July appointing General Krstic commander of the Drina Corps, because it is only the president who has the authority to appoint people to these strategic groupings and positions. While we were at Zepa, whether it was over the media or in some other way, anyway, we learnt of the decree of the president of the republic. And I know that sometime around the 20th of July or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thereabouts, there was a gathering of generals in a facility close to Han Pijesak. There were a number of generals from the Main Staff and the commanders of the other Corps, and also present were General Zivanovic and General Krstic, and I know that the event was organised to observe the handover of duty by the commander of the Drina Corps. And I know that after General Krstic's return to the forward command post in the village of Godenje, some people congratulated him on his taking over of duty. I wish to mention that in that period we were at a location which had very little information outside those related to the combat operations in Zepa and around it, and General Krstic himself did not talk about his appointment with us other officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're an officer who has graduated from the highest military educational institutions that existed in the former Yugoslavia and in the newly formed republics. According to your laws and regulations, the takeover of duty, is it an obligatory act that has to take place when commanders change, regardless of the level of command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to our laws and regulations, it is prescribed in detail that all duties in the army, from the lowest to the highest level, have a date fixed when one officer hands over duty to the other and all the obligations, the documents, the material consequences resulting from that position. And after this period, which is defined clearly by their superior, a document has to be compiled with a defined content, and that document is called a record on the handing over and taking over of duty. So it has a clearly defined format according to instructions, and only after that report has been drafted, this is the basic document which serves as a basis for the drafting of other documents such as the taking over of duty and other personnel papers. So that the person taking over of duty, once these documents come into effect, in fact becomes what he has been appointed to become by his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us depart for a moment from our main topic, that is, Srebrenica and this time period, and let me ask you a general question. As you are a military officer, and one can assume that you are knowledgeable about these things, the regular combat report from subordinate units when addressed to the superior command, who receives these reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regular operative combat report from subordinate units, if they are being sent by teletype encoded links, reach the communications centre; and if they are sent by courier or messenger, they are delivered to the mailing department, from where they are carried to the operations room or the operations centre of the Corps command, the reception of which is confirmed by signature to the carrier in his book by the operations officer on duty or the duty officer in the operations centre, so he signs this book confirming receipt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the operations officer on duty is the first person to familiarise himself with the contents of such reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the framework of the daily functioning of control and command, it is clearly defined up to what time those reports have to be delivered, so that the operations officer on duty will have time to round off all those reports and make a compilation of them and send an operations report of that command to the superior command. Once he has drafted such a report, he takes it to the commander for his inspection, and on that occasion he may draw his attention to something that may be new, that deviates from the regular situation regarding the unit's reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the proceedings so far, we have seen a great deal of markings, and I don't want to put them on the ELMO, but I'm going to give you an example. For example, Zlatar 1 as a name, and 01. Can you explain to us what that means, Zlatar 1 and 01?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions with regard to documents related to communications is precisely defined in a document which is called a review of code names, and it is there to protect the names of the actual units. For example, if we're talking about the command of the Drina Corps as the actual name and title of the unit, then its code name should be Zlatar. Then in going through the other code names and a review of them, it states that the rear command post is Zlatar 1, that the forward command post is Zlatar 2. And if we define a reserve command post, if that is defined as well and stipulated, then that could be Zlatar 3. In the rules and regulations that exist in the army, the mark "01" or "02" does not exist anywhere, although in wartime practice it is frequently used to -- that is to say, the commanding officers who are commanders or chiefs or suchlike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, I should now like to show you some intercepts, radio messages intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I call upon the usher for Exhibit -- OTP Exhibit 698A bis. Would you please put it on the ELMO, the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, Witness DB, would you please read through this intercept, radio message. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember in the course of the time you spent at the forward command post of Zepa, do you remember having had this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was some 150, 200 soldiers which were to have been pulled out of the composition of forces which took part in the Zepa operation and that they were to be deployed to the vicinity of Han Pijesak, not far from Zepa, in order to ensure certain communications or to set up some ambushes, because at that time, that is to say, during that period, we expected a breakthrough by the forces of the 285th Zepa Brigade from the direction of Zepa towards Han Pijesak and Kladanj. I remember this because I thought at the time how I could organise communications with that unit, which was going a little further off from the area of the combat operations themselves. But I don't remember -- here there's -- there's a question here which I don't seem to remember. It says, "Is Jokic there?" "Is Jokic around?" That's what the question is: "Is Jokic around?" And I'm quite certain that there wasn't any Jokic there at the time, if that is the conversation and the period. There wasn't a Jokic there at all at Krivace or Godenje either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher now to place OTP Exhibit 477A bis on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, just a question. This intercepted message, do you have it by any chance in an audio cassette?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, do you know who Major Furtula is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Furtula at the time was the commander of the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Tasic and Sladojevic are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the individuals Nastic and Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the commanders of the brigades of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who Ljubo Beara is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, during the time you spent at the forward command post, see Ljubo Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay at the forward command post, did you hear through your communications systems about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody, any of your soldiers, signalsmen, convey to you the fact that he was -- his presence in the radio relay communications network?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like now to ask the usher for OTP Exhibit 786A, B. For purposes of the record, Mr. President, the Defence would like to take note that this exhibit has still not been admitted into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just looking in the record. I heard the English translation of 786, and I believe the exhibit that my colleague is referring to is 789.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, it has not been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, 789.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, do you remember that you had a conversation during your stay at the forward command post in which stocari are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had different conversations and different messages were conveyed. I know that most of them referred to combat activities, and nothing with regard to stocari, cowboys or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as this document has not been introduced into evidence, the Defence will withdraw it, but just used it to ask this one question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, you spent a lot of your time with the communications system and systems. You have a lot of experience and knowledge about what we call intercepts, intercepts of radio-relayed messages. What is your knowledge in that respect as to the possibility of interception, the transcription, and the whole technique, and the general reliability?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If the witness is going to testify as an expert, then I believe we should have received a report of this witness as an expert in the subject area about which he's going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has posed certain restrictions with respect to asking these questions. Of course, we're not going to ask the witness to -- who is present here to speak as an expert witness. That was not our intention. We just wanted to hear his opinion, and I don't think that comes under the rules and regulations of expert witness testimony at all. We're just asking for an opinion in view of the fact that he spent some time at that forward command post and did a lot of work with radio communications, that he heard many conversations and so on and so forth, and just to present us with his views about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean you want to ask him only about his own experience, what he has been doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with respect to the conversations that he has been presented with so far during his examination and testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the testimony is limited to his experience only, then that's a different issue; but if he's testifying as an expert, then under the appropriate rule, we should have received an expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, only his own experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only his own experience, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the functioning of communications goes and their protection, radio communication and monitoring and interception in this past war, what I can say is that the situation was the following: Those monitoring groups listening in were formed, or perhaps 100 per cent they were formed of people who do not have the necessary experience required in the army. They were not trained for that work in the army or in military schools. They were not trained to do that work, but they learnt to do it as they went along while they were monitoring and intercepting certain lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, you are speaking of the people intercepting on your side, on the Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not what you call the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in preparing for this trial, I had occasion to read through some of the intercepts by our enemies, and I have come to the conclusion that they worked along the lines that we worked too. The way we worked was similar. So what I say for our side can also -- is also true of the other side, the enemy side. But I'd just like to mention, having said that, that the enemy side had far worse military technology in that area and that they had to resort to improvisation using other technical devices. But I do know that it was very difficult to monitor and intercept certain communication lines, especially radio relay ones, because, as a rule, one participant in the conversation would be heard much clearer than the other; the other one would be very weak or hardly audible at all. So that it was on the basis of recollections and assumptions as to what that party could say. This was inscribed as the message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one question, if I could, Witness DB. I want to make sure I understand your testimony. If, if there were mistakes or if an intercept didn't accurately reflect what had actually been said between the parties, where is it most likely the mistake would have been made? On the side of the monitoring person who was listening, who didn't understand, or -- I mean, where is it most likely that the thing went wrong, if in fact at the end the intercept didn't reflect what actually went on in the conversation? Where is the most likely area that it would have broken down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my experience, most probably where it would have broken down would be the individual monitoring the conversation, because, as a rule, those conversations are taped and then they are transcribed and recorded on the basis of what is listened to and heard. And as the audibility and clarity of the material that has been recorded is on the limits or borderline of what can be used or not, then very often the people monitoring and intercepting, based on a certain logics of their own or based on previously intercepted conversations and what they heard previously, determine who the speakers could be and what was said approximately. According to our regulations, those individuals would have had to have spent five years doing that type of work to be considered competent to sift through the correct information from the incorrect, and the important and unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has reached the end of their examination of this witness. We have one or two more questions, but may we suggest that this be done in private session, in view of the fact that the questions emanate from questions that have already been answered during this trial in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no further questions for Witness DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you like to start your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you like to start your cross-examination after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask: Do you have another witness for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: For this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We have no more witnesses, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you give us more information about the condition of General Krstic when you come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, and this is a question that the Defence did wish to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you come back, we expect that. Thank you. May I just ask Mr. Harmon: How long would you think your cross-examination will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe my cross-examination will conclude tomorrow, sometime in the middle of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Tomorrow. Good. So let's have a break for 20 minutes. Thank you. So we come back here at a quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you start your cross-examination, I don't want to limit you with time. Usually I prefer not to make the break before you finish a series of questioning, but as you saw, I wouldn't like it to be more than an hour and a quarter maximum, or even one hour, and then we have a break. But I don't want it to be hard and fast rules; otherwise, there will be an interruption, and unless one of the main features -- or the main players in our trial is disturbed, is indisposed, we can continue till an hour or an hour and a quarter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just wanted to mention that I just received a statement from General Krstic that he has no objections to the Court proceedings continuing in his absence. So I have it here, and it will be Exhibit D133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Petrusic also if he has any news about his medical condition?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break, Mr. President, we spoke to General Krstic, and he is waiting for the surgery to take place in the course of the day. Whether this will be carried out in the Detention Unit or somewhere else, we don't know that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you have more information about the surgery itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing more than that, except as far as we have been informed, an incision has to be made to remove the blood clot, which will mean that he will have to rest for the next few days, and probably he will be unable to attend the proceedings, but that raises another issue. In view of the fact that we will probably be completing the examination of this witness tomorrow, after that comes the re-examination of General Krstic by the Prosecution and by Your Honours. In view of his medical condition now and after this surgical intervention, we doubt that that examination will be possible, so may I take the liberty to suggest to the Trial Chamber that this part of the proceedings should take place in the following sitting which has been scheduled to begin on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean the examination of General Krstic by the Prosecution and the Judges? And what about your other witnesses? You have no other witnesses at all this week or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For this week, we have no other witnesses. We had too many at one point, and they were waiting for quite a long time. And in collaboration with the Witness and Victim's Unit, we came to the conclusion it would be best to send them home, and then for the next sitting after the 20th of November, we could have them brought here to testify. In the meantime, again, for the Trial Chamber's information, the Defence has revised the list of witnesses in relation to the list submitted on the 14th of October so that we will be able to fit into the time frame set by the Trial Chamber for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for all your cooperation. Please convey our best wishes to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Riad and Judge Wald. Just to inform you, throughout this examination I will be asking for private sessions on a number of occasions because of the necessity to ensure the protection of this witness's identity. And if I could right away ask for a private session so as not to disclose this witness's identity, I intend to ask him some questions that may well expose his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please call.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, I'm going to be asking you questions about the events that took place in Srebrenica and the events that took place in Zepa from early July to August of 1995. I will be also asking you about events that took place after that. And those events took place many years ago. Witness DB, did you keep a notebook and record any events or any significant communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony before this Trial Chamber is based on your recollections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to coming to this Trial Chamber to testify, did you have an opportunity to review any documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What documents did you review?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at a part of the documents shown to me by Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the documents shown to you by Mr. Petrusic, did you review any other documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since February, or rather April this year, connected to all the events that took place in the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, I communicated quite frequently with people I knew and who were participants in the event, and in this way I refreshed my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you identify the people with whom you communicated in order to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly officers from the Drina Corps and a number of soldiers, signalsmen who were with me at Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Can you identify them by name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Colonel Vicic, with Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic, and two of my signalsmen soldiers. One is called Baki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the other one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other one is Plakalovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have first names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plakalovic's first name is Mirko. And as for the other one, we usually use his nickname, so I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember his first name or his surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two of them, twin brothers. One of them was with me. The name of one of them is Momir, but you see, I'm not sure, because there are two of them, two twin brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you talk to anybody else about the events in Srebrenica and Zepa besides the four individuals you've identified for us today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did with a lot of people, but these are customary conversations amongst us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Witness DB, is: In order to prepare for your testimony today, you've identified four people with whom you talked in order to refresh your recollection. My question to you is: Did you talk to any other individuals other than the four you have identified today in order to refresh your recollection about the events that occurred in Srebrenica and in Zepa in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that we often communicate amongst ourselves over there and that I spoke to a number of people, but not in the context, strictly speaking, of my preparations for my testimony, but rather when we commented on those events and that time period and the consequences those events have had, so I cannot specify the people I actually spoke to as part of the preparations for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness DB, we'll move on to a different topic, then. Let me ask you: Who is the Drina Corps chief of communications and electronic security? Who was he in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a position and term in the corps that was called chief of communications and not commander for security and communications, if we are referring to the same position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are. And who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Nedo Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, again, referring to 1D, Lieutenant Colonel Nedo Blagojevic appears at this location in the section dealing with the corps staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention, Witness DB, on the role of mister -- or Lieutenant Colonel Nedo Blagojevic. Can you describe to the Trial Chamber his role, his duties and responsibilities, and his relationship with the higher officers within the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have asked me a very wide-ranging question, so could you please cut it up into parts?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd be glad to. Can you tell me about the role of Lieutenant Colonel Nedo Blagojevic in the Drina Corps command structure? What was his role? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of communications of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did being chief of communications of the corps entail? What were his job responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of communications is a member of the staff of the corps, and in a sense, he's a professional advisory body for the area of communications. According to the chain of command, he's subordinate to the Chief of Staff, and his duties are wide ranging and prescribed by the rules, and they mainly entail organising, establishing, and functioning and protection of all communications in the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Lieutenant Colonel Blagojevic was a subordinate to General Krstic who, prior to the 13th of July, was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military sense, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as an advisor to General Krstic, he would inform him, advise him of important aspects that related to communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it should be. Now, whether he informed him and briefed him on these things, I don't know, because I wasn't present at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But that's the way it should have worked in the system of the army of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could go back into private session very briefly for one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Private session, if you please. Mr. Harmon, I have a name here. I have a name called Vidoje Blagojevic, Vidoje Blagojevic. It's another person?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Vidoje Blagojevic was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, so there are two Blagojevics on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, I want to ask you about the creation of a communications plan for a military operation. You have been in the VRS and were in the VRS, and participated in a number of military operations. Can you tell the Judges of this Trial Chamber how a communications plan is created, why it is created, and how it is ultimately distributed for implementation. If you would walk us through the steps of the procedure, I would be very appreciative. Let us start, for ease of your reference, let us start with the commander of the Drina Corps and his idea. He has an idea. He wants to perhaps commence an operation against a specific target, and he wants a communications plan. Would you walk us through how that communications plan is developed, reviewed, ratified, and then implemented.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Corps Commander is given an assignment by his superior -- I'm now speaking in purely theoretical terms -- he first studies the assignment given to him himself. Then he convenes his closest associates, members of his staff, and together with them, he reviews the assignment and develops the basic concept for the implementation of that assignment. After that, the whole staff gets together or all the professionals who can contribute to the creation of the plan and the implementation of the assignment, and they are all informed of this basic concept. A plan of work for the command is created, and then all those professionals are duty-bound within a certain time period to prepare proposals for the commander for the implementation of that assignment, of course, each one of them within their own areas of competence and their own jurisdiction and in line with their duties and responsibilities. To be more specific, the chief of communications, because that was the focus of your question. He is now aware of the concept and the idea of the commander. He knows what the technical and personnel capabilities are of the Communications Battalion as a unit that can implement that assignment in the communications area. And the chief of communications, on the basis of that information, prepares a draft proposal for the organisation of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. communications. Once all the professionals and assistant commanders and the assistant of the Chief of Staff have drafted their proposals for a decision to be made, then they all meet again and, according to their plan of work, they present their proposals, either to the Chief of Staff or to the commander directly. On the basis of all the proposals that serve as a basis for the decision-making, the Chief of Staff drafts the proposal of the decision itself, and it can have several versions, and he presents it to the Corps Commander. The Corps Commander approves one of the drafts. He may add something or delete something, according to his own judgement, and then he announces the decision. The decision is then drafted in written form and it becomes law as such in its written form. Once the decision has been announced, all the assistant commanders and assistants to the Chief of Staff within their areas of responsibility prepare the executive documents of the operations plan. The chief of communications drafts the communications plan, which consists of several documents. That communications plan is approved by the Chief of Staff or the Corps Commander and then that plan is forwarded to the Communications Battalion and to subordinate units and their communications units. I have told you now in brief the theory and one of the methods of work of the command, as we were taught in schools and which it is desirable to implement in practice whenever there is time and whenever the situation allows it. I wish to underline that our wartime practice in many ways deviated from these rules precisely because of the lack of time, the impossibility of gathering in one place at the same time all the assistants and other professionals from the various different segments, because our units were drawn out along the front lines and within the rear, carrying out various assignments. And I also wish to note that this was the year 1995, when the command and officer cadres already had a great deal of experience, and only a few input information was required by all the assistants for them to be able to act more speedily than the theory envisages the procedure to take and which I have tried to describe to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your description of the theory of how a communications plan is created, as I understood it, it appears that the -- after the commander has his original idea, the advisors or the assistants to the command, including the chief of communications, go their separate ways. They draft proposals and they present their proposals initially to either the Chief of Staff or to the commander directly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the term means to propose, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then the Chief of Staff reviews the proposals and prepares a proposal that he himself presents to the commander, with various options, with variations that the commander himself can select; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the theory of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the commander makes a choice and the assistants are informed of that choice, and they finalise a plan of communications in this case that they again present to the Chief of Staff or to the commander for approval; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understand. Thank you. Now, at the time -- before the Srebrenica operation was launched on the 6th of July, 1995, the Chief of Staff was General Krstic and the commander of the Drina Corps was General Zivanovic; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 428.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness DB, 428 is the order to activate combat activities in Srebrenica. Have you seen this document prior to coming to court to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the document. It was with Mr. Petrusic. But as far as any details and more profound analysis goes, I did not undertake that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite all right. Now, this document, as you can see, Witness DB, identifies where this particular order is being sent, does it not? In the top part of this document it identifies "To the commands of". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this plan to attack Srebrenica involved multiple subordinate units of the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to -- on this exhibit I believe it's on page 3 in the B/C/S. Toward the bottom paragraph, there is identified a reserve force of the size of two or three companies of the MUP and one company from the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior and the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, those were elements that were to be included in the attack on Srebrenica, although as reserve units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you, Witness DB: Was a communications plan created for operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: A communications plan for this particular operation I do not think was drafted with all the documents that that implied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is -- when you say with all of the documents that that implied, would you tell us what all of the documents that a communications plan implied means? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of communications in those documents, that is to say, that responsibility, he would have to write out an order for communications, as it is called. Furthermore, he would have to write an order for marching and for the actual establishment of the communications centre. Additional documents would be required for all the radio networks and radio relay directions that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are any other documents included in a communications plan besides the three documents that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a schematic for radio communication and things of that kind, a review of the code names, a review of the numbers for identifying the commanding officers, a schematic for the courier links, as well as the crypto-protection documents and other similar documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a communications plan for Krivaja 95 was created, would that plan have been reviewed by General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, that would be what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have described in brief what is normally included in a full, robust communications plan. Was an abbreviated communications plan created for Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, yes, because otherwise communications could not have been set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review that abbreviated plan for Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably received -- I don't actually remember. I probably received a plan for the radio communications. As for the other details, I really do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I made some notes while you were testifying, and you mentioned something about a review of code names would be included in a communications plan. Does that mean that the various units that were to participate in the attack on Srebrenica under Operation Krivaja 95 were given code names so they could communicate with each other during the operation itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the radio network of command, everybody had certain code names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all of the tactical units that were going to participate in the attack on Srebrenica as well as the reserve units that I've identified in the -- or that are identified in the Krivaja 95 plan were given code names, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a plan had been drawn up, in keeping with this order in which, among other things, the reserve units are stated, then most probably in a plan of that kind, the code names should have been included for all the units and reserve units. I do not remember whether that plan was actually drafted, and as I told you a moment ago, on the basis of our experience and the practical knowledge we gained, many of the things were done based precisely on experience and as an ongoing process as we progressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness DB, the units that were to participate in the attack on Srebrenica would have been informed of their code names prior to the operation itself being launched; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the operation itself began, I'm quite certain that they would have to have had a document, and that would have been the plan for radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the next exhibit, it is Prosecutor's Exhibit 776, if that could be shown to the witness, please. Madam Registrar, do you have exhibits to distribute to the Judges and Defence? The Defence apparently does not have a copy of Prosecutor's Exhibit 776. Could we have just a moment, Your Honours? I had assumed that these were available for Your Honours' viewing as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness DB, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness DB, I just want more clarification. When you said that you don't recall that a plan was actually drafted and many of the things were done based on experience and on ongoing process as the progressed, you mean the experience of whom, of the soldiers or of the commanders? There was still orders given and plans made, or what? Or everybody did what he felt -- what his experience told him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commanding did exist, and I said that it was necessary to have some input information, basic input information. I don't know whether you followed me there. So some necessary pieces of information as input, and then everybody was able to do his job on the basis of that. And for example, for me, it was always enough to know where the forward command post would be and which units would take part, so those are just two pieces of information; and third, when the communications had been established, needed to be established. I didn't have to be told anything more than that. So that's what I had in mind. This type of command did exist. The commanding officers did their work and the other officers, but the steps necessary were reduced to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is a document that was seized pursuant to a lawful search warrant issued by the Trial Chamber, and it was seized at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. Now, if we could have the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, you can see in the upper right-hand corner of that document it says "strictly confidential," and it says "Krivaja 95." Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says, "This is a work schedule for radio network No. 122." Now, does this appear to be part of the communications plan that was distributed to, in this case, the Bratunac Brigade prior to the commencement of the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're going to review this document together. On the top of the large box that is divided there are a series of words, the first being "user," and I take it, Witness DB, that "user" refers to the user of the communications within the work plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next column is the code name, and is this the code name that was given to the various users identified in the previous column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we go in the user column, for example, to the third box down, we see the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade was given the code name of Ruma, R-u-m-a; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go down further, we see that the Ministry of the Interior, one of the reserve units of this operation, was given the code name Oblak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then all of the participating units have been identified. Now, there appears to be at the bottom something called a reserve user, and that appears twice, and there are two code names next to reserve user. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber the meaning of reserve user, and why reserve user was given code names? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct you, Mr. Prosecutor, on one point. You said here that the planned participants who did take part, as far as I recall, that it says the users who took part in the operation. These are users who have been planned for the operation pursuant to the order which is here, which means that the chief of communications, as in the order I don't think it says anything about the organisation of communications with respect to this operation, then probably the chief of communications just read through the order and saw who the possible participants were and then drew up a plan of this kind. So these are the possible users, those who have been planned, but not the ones who might actually have taken part. And now let me explain what "reserve user" means, which is what you asked me. Whenever a plan of work, a work schedule for radio networks is compiled, always, not just for one particular operation, but always, two to four or five reserve users are provided for, and they are reserve names. That is to say, if one of the units -- if a unit were to be included into the combat operations and not provided for by the plan, or subsequently, and the other users in that network can identify the unit, that the unit is in fact engaged in the same assignment, so our rules always provide for the fact that we have some reserve users, and this document is an example. And there are always two to five reserve users.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a contingency plan. In the event additional units are needed in the operation, they have a code name and they can be inserted into the plan itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: They need not be units should the need arise. It can be different types of users, for example, a radio relay interim station or one that also takes part as a mediator in providing communications. So that is usually provided for so that the plan is made more effective and efficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the term "reserve user" can be a unit of soldiers, a group of soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it can also refer to a series of other subjects or participants in this particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Witness DB. Thank you. Now, you earlier said that all of these units that have been identified were given their code names prior to the operation itself commencing. I take it, Witness DB, that the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps was fully aware that Ministry of the Interior units were going to participate in Operation Krivaja 95 as a reserve component; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that you assume that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that General Krstic, who was the Chief of Staff and who in theory would have reviewed the communications plan, was aware that the Ministry of the Interior forces that are identified in this exhibit were going to participate in the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify matters with respect to your question. Whenever an operation was planned for a certain area, whether it be combat operations, a battle, or anything else, and I'm talking about tactical levels, whether companies or battalions or brigades take part in that particular operation, and whether the assignment is an attack, or whether it is to search the terrain, or whether it is defence of the terrain, or whether it is reconnaissance or any other type of activity, every commander gave thought to the units he could deploy from the area, so that MUP was something that was always reckoned with as the idea was collaborated. And in practice, because of their responsibilities, that is to say, their duties in town with respect to safety for persons and property and traffic regulation and everything else that MUP was engaged in, we never actually counted on the possibility of having them be reinforcements in any given operation. And on the basis of the whole of my experience during the war, I recall MUP units taking part only on two occasions. That is to say that they were together with the other units in an operation on a footing of equality, as equal participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, you have seen Krivaja 95, and the MUP is identified, along with the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, as a reserve unit. In Prosecutor's Exhibit 776 they are identified and given a code name. My question to you, Witness DB, was: Was General Krstic, in your opinion, aware of the participation and role of the MUP in Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was not. May I explain that? May I explain why that is my opinion? Because I have reviewed this plan. All these other things do not belong to communications that you have given me. These code names and this table are prepared by operations bodies, and they are special encryption documents that have to do with coded maps and the transmission of information by encrypted signs. I spoke about all this before you gave me this document. And anyway, Mr. Petrusic did not show it to me. All we had was this as communications. But let me answer your question. I know for a fact that we at the forward command post at the village of Pribicevac and in the villages of Krivace and Godenje did not have MUP units linked to us and that General Krstic could not communicate with them, regardless of where they were, because they were not a component part of the operation. And I know also for sure that all these other participants -- all this is based on my recollection, because I didn't have a chance to look at this document, but I know for a fact that General Krstic did not have command over MUP units and that they were here only planned at the beginning if need be, as potential participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they were planned in the operation as it was originally envisioned, MUP is identified again in the communications plan that was distributed to all of the participants, and my question is: Was General Krstic again aware of their participation and role in the plan prior to Krivaja 95 commencing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me turn to the next page of this document, and you should -- do you have that in B/C/S in front of you? It is a column starting in the upper left-hand corner with the upper box 102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. I just want to ask the witness about what he meant by they were meant -- the MUP was planned as a potential participant. If they are a potential participant, when they participate, would they be under the authority of General Krstic when they participate effectively?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can say is that on the basis of the order in which it is stated, among others, that MUP forces are designated as reserve units, so the chief of communications made a plan accordingly. What was in the mind of the person who made this plan and what he had in mind at the time, I really don't know; I cannot know. All I know is that from the forward command post there was no communication with them. They were not in the network with us. No commands could be issued to them from the forward command post, because I was next to the equipment and they were not one of the participants in the radio network, so I don't see how any commands could be issued to them from the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we've concluded with this document. I'm not sure the part that I wanted to refer to is included in this particular document. So we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm finished with that, Cedric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if you're starting a new line of questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- we can make a break here. As I previously explained, I'm not trying to impose strict time limits, but in general, I will suggest that we resume after 45 minutes, which means at 40 minutes past 12.00. And then we can continue for an hour, till 1.40, and then resume at 2.00 till 3.00. Of course, this is, as I said, flexible, because I don't want to interrupt a coherent line of questions. We can stop a little bit before or a little bit after, but without any abuse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So we adjourn till 12.00 -- 12.40. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please resume, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, the MUP Special Police are part of the Ministry of the Interior, are they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 185 and 186, please, given to the witness. If they could be placed on the ELMO. If we could start with Prosecutor's exhibit -- let me see which number that is, Mr. Usher. That first one you have in your hand, Mr. Usher, I'm not sure of the exhibit number of that. THE USHER: 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 185 is placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I cannot see the number on his sleeve, but I think it could be General Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what unit is he a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I think that his name is linked to the special units that you mentioned. I'm not sure of that, but I think that his name is being linked to those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Court has heard testimony, Witness DB, that this man was a member of the MUP Special Police. Do you have any reason to disagree with that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that the MUP Special Police was in Potocari on the 11th. General Krstic testified to that fact. My question to you is, first, when you travelled through Potocari on the evening of the 11th and arrived in Bratunac, did you see members of the MUP Special Police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Witness DB, that the MUP Special Police was organising themselves in and around the area of Zuti Most, the Yellow Bridge, the bridge which you passed over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the participation of MUP units in the operation of Srebrenica, I know the following, if I may tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, answer my question first, and then we may return to what you know, but ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I know that there were some people at the locality of Zuti Most, at the checkpoint which earlier was the defensive position of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. I'm referring to the asphalt road. And I know that as I was moving from Potocari towards Bratunac via Zuti Most, that I did see there some men. In my judgement, this must have been around 2130 hours. It was already dark. I do not remember whether they were just soldiers or only the police, or both soldiers and the police together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could have, Mr. Usher, the next photograph placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this photograph, Witness DB, do you see Mr. Borovcanin once again standing next to the man with the United Nations helmet on his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that the picture on the monitor is rather hazy, and I wouldn't dare to make a final judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has seen evidence of MUP Special Police operating along the Bratunac-Milici road. There is film footage of this that has been presented to the Trial Chamber where Mr. Borovcanin, who is in the picture before you, and other members of his unit are along that road. You travelled that road on the night of the 11th, Witness DB. Did you see members of the MUP Special Police along that road when you travelled it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the -- I answered in the affirmative a question put by Mr. Petrusic to me yesterday that moving from Bratunac towards Vlasenica, after 2300 hours on the 11th of July, on the road Bratunac-Kravica-Konjevic Polje, in several places I saw members wearing blue uniforms, and those were the uniforms of the MUP at the time. Now, whether when I was passing the Yellow Bridge, Zuti Most, whether they were there also mixed together with soldiers or whether there were only soldiers there, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit 499A, the B/C/S version 499B given to the witness. And 499A placed on the ELMO, and in the English version, Mr. Usher, I would like page 3 placed on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, if the witness could be shown this page with the tank, in that page of the article. If you could place page 3 of this article on the ELMO, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, this is an article that was written -- it is dated the 21st of July, 1995, in a Belgrade publication. Its author is a gentleman named Zoran Petrovic. The Trial Chamber has seen a film that was taken during the events in Potocari and Srebrenica throughout the days of the attack and the events that took place along the Bratunac-Milici road that was prepared by this very same author, Zoran Petrovic. Now, I'd like to direct your attention, please, Witness, to the article that is in front of you in B/C/S. And if you would please refer to this section that I have highlighted and which I hope you can see from where you are, and read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read that, Witness DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean have I read it before?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This section of the article that I have directed your attention to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this portion that I would like to read into the record is as follows. This is on page 3: "In less than three days of fighting, Mladic's forces reached the suburbs of the enclave, and on the fourth day they had fully taken over Srebrenica. After the main attack, RS MUP forces, commanded by Ljubisa Borovcanin, struck along the Zuti List-Potocari line and were advancing toward Djogazi and Milacevici from the right side." Now, Witness, it appears from this article that the MUP, Ministry of the Interior Special Police, were engaged in a capacity of combat in this particular article, does it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this article. Whoever reads this article would come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the MUP special police that are referred to in this article are consistent with the Ministry of the Interior forces that are described in Krivaja 95 communications plan that you saw prior to adjourning for lunch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the plan is one thing and the actual implementation quite another. We had an identical plan to this one for the Zepa operation, and immediately after the first day the Zvornik Brigade was pulled out of that operation, but its position in the plan remained. I don't know how you come to the conclusion that on the basis of the communications plan, where MUP was planned, that that was this very unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything in this plan that indicates it is not, Witness DB? Anything in this communications plan that indicates that it is not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that then, in this communications plan, it should have said "the special MUP units" if before the combat operation started it had been known that that particular special unit would be participating, because that was the only special MUP brigade, and then it would have been included in the plan. If I may take the liberty of saying, when MUP was mentioned in all our plans, the reference was to local public security stations in the local communities. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Krivaja 95, which is an order to attack the Srebrenica enclave and identifies a reserve force and it identifies the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade as one of those reserve forces and the MUP, those forces were reserves for combat activities, weren't they, Witness DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: When reserves are being regulated, reserves can be used for several options. They can be used to blockade a certain area, to establish control over a certain area, or simply for inclusion in combat operations after the main forces had accomplished their task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move to a different topic, Witness DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Harmon. Before we leave the MUP members, I just want a clarification, because Witness DB, you mentioned that on the 11th of July, at 11.00 p.m., you saw, when you were moving from Bratunac to Vlasenica, you saw MUP members in blue uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then as you passed the Yellow Bridge, the Zuti Most, I think, which is, I suppose, at the same time, you don't remember having seen anything. They were in blue uniform? They were distinguishable from others or were they mixed up in a crowd which you couldn't distinguish? You remember the first one, and this is linked with it. What made the difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to explain. While I was moving from Pribicevac via Srebrenica and Potocari to Bratunac, about 2100 hours I passed through Zuti Most. This is quite a different route. On that Zuti Most, which is close to the town of Srebrenica, or Potocari, which is between Bratunac and Potocari, I noticed on that part of the road where defensive positions of the Bratunac Brigade used to be towards Srebrenica, I saw men in uniform. I cannot now say with certainty whether they were only soldiers, only MUP, or both, because I just drove past them. This was a small group of people next to the road. And when after the meeting that was held in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters I headed towards Krivace -- or rather, Vlasenica, this was after 2300 hours, in quite a different area, the route from Bratunac via Krivace, Konjevic Polje, Kasaba Milici, towards Vlasenica, this is an entirely different area along the road at several points, and that is why I paid more attention because I saw several groups. I did notice members of MUP. I saw them along the road, and I registered in my mind these blue-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Witness DB, it's your position that in the Srebrenica attack plan, the reserve forces of the MUP that are designated here were traffic police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that, as far as I recall. I didn't say it was the traffic police. I have knowledge that the unit which was -- which has been identified, that it was part of the Srebrenica operation, and that it came one or two days prior to the military fall of Srebrenica, which means that that was around the 10th of July, and that it did have some assignments in the area ranging from Bratunac, that is to say, from the north to the south of the enclave. I was very interested in seeing whether it would be necessary to establish communication with them because they were coming from quite a different direction, and therefore I was interested in seeing where they were coming from, when they arrived, and whether they would have -- whether we would need to establish communication with them, because for me as a signalsman, this was a very vital point. I had to ensure that there was -- that communication should not upset control and command. I do know that with that particular MUP unit which was there on the spot and which probably, based on all the material that we have and that you have shown me and which I, too, became acquainted, that -- and that it was commanded by General Borovcanin. We did not have any communications with them. I'm thinking about the forward command post, from the forward command post from which General Krstic was in command of that operation. We did not have that unit on the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to the signalsman from the MUP Special Police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because they never had within their composition the kind of devices that we have, and I didn't see him at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of devices did they have?
