utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they mostly used devices on the UKT wave band, ultra short, and to facilitate interpretation, these were known as the Motorolas because of the firm that produced those devices, Motorola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different topic. Let's turn to the forward command post and the location of Pribicevac, and what I'd like to ask you first off is, this was a village, wasn't it? This wasn't a swath of territory cut out of a virgin forest for purposes of the forward command post, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a former Serbian village which in the spring of 1992 had been burnt and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Pribicevac, did you happen to see a man by the name of Vukota Vukovic at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what his position was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vukota Vukovic was on behalf of the corps command sent to the Pribicevac area, Pribicevac area. I think that that was a year or so before the Krivaja-5 operation, and I do believe that he had the assignment of coordinating the defence positions of the Skelani Battalion and the Bratunac Brigade in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he the commander of the Skelani Separate Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a commander of the Skelani Separate Battalion by the name of Vukota Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me first of all start with Prosecutor's Exhibit 821. If the witness -- Mr. Usher, if the witness could be shown the B/C/S version and the English version placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, take a moment to examine this document, and let me know when you have finished your review. Now, the content of this document, Witness, is not important; however, the captions in this document are important. In the upper left-hand corner you will see in this document that's dated 19 April 1994 a reference to the Pribicevac Tactical Group 1, and at the bottom of this you will see that the commander of that group was Colonel Vukota Vukovic. Are you familiar with the Pribicevac Tactical Group No. 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our rules and regulations, the ones that were in force with respect to the grouping of forces, implied the establishment of combat groups and tactical groups. Combat groups are of a smaller composition, not more than the rank of battalion, and they are established for the execution of a limited combat operation. Tactical groups are groups of the armed forces of a battalion-type composition, and they are a provisional composition having the task of uniting and coordinating action of -- the action of several battalions or several brigades. I think that to all intents and purposes, the Pribicevac Tactical Group did exist, precisely with the task of coordinating action of what -- the action of one to two battalions of the Bratunac Brigade, I think in the area ranging from Kvarc or Pribicevac via Kvarc towards Zuti Most, and the operations of the Skelani Battalion which covered the area to the left and right of the river Zeleni Jadar, and that it served as a coordinator. And as the commander of that tactical group at Pribicevac in the period that I mentioned, that Colonel Vukota Vukovic was sent there to command, from the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the next exhibit which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 822, and if this Exhibit could be placed under seal. And Your Honour, if we could go into private session in respect of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, let's go.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you left the Pribicevac Forward Command Post, it continued to exist, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 11th of July now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about after you left on the 2nd of November, 1994. Did the Pribicevac Forward Command Post continue to exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a forward command post; it was a command post of the Pribicevac Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next Exhibit, please, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 824. Mr. Usher, if you could place the first page of the English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a document that is dated the 4th of June, 1995. It is signed by the commander of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic. And in the top part, left-hand side of the document, you can see that this document was issued from the Pribicevac Forward Command Post on the 4th of June, 1995, and it is an order for the deployment of units in the defence of the region of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. What can you tell us, Witness DB, about the Pribicevac Forward Command Post of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a time period -- that is to say, it's the beginning of June, 1995, and according to my recollections, I said yesterday that I was there at the beginning of June, when in that particular region [inaudible] communication was established for Zeleni Jadar, Jasenova, and Podravanje, and placed under the control of our own forces, and quite simply by rounding off and encircling that part of the territory and placing it under our control, and this was determined by the peace agreement for that particular period. I had to be there at the time because we're dealing with the beginning of June. And these assignments were compiled by Colonel Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and he probably at that time had reached Pribicevac and himself had established his own forward command post at Pribicevac for the implementation of the assignment issued to him by the corps command. It is quite possible that during that period of time when General Zivanovic was at Pribicevac himself, that there were two forward command posts there at the time, one forward command post of the Bratunac Brigade as it says here in this document, and another forward command post, a provisional forward command post of the Drina Corps for the duration of that assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, paragraph 4 reads as follows: "The commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion shall incorporate this company in the battalion's command and control system, and with the assistance of the brigade's chief of communication organise wire and radio communication with this company." Now, once again there's reference to communications at this location; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right, communications are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the last document in this series; it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 823.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, I see, Your Honours, and for my friends at the Defence bench, this is out of sequence. This is a document that is one month earlier than the previous document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this also is a document that was issued by General Zivanovic on the 12th of May, 1995, to the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and to the Skelani Independent Infantry Battalion. And if you turn to the order itself, paragraph 3 of the order -- which is on page 2, Mr. Usher, of the English version -- paragraph 3 reads, "The command of the Skelani Separate Battalion will immediately establish an IKM, a forward command post, in the village of Jasenova and provide from there secure telephone and packet communication links with the command of the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade." Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what the English translation of it says. Perhaps you had a --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. In the official document that I have, and it is a copy of the original, it says that telephone and courier communication should be secured, not packet communication, with the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Light Infantry Brigade and not with the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, we will have this submitted once again, Your Honours, to the language service section that translated it in the first place, and we can resolve that issue. We stand by correct and accurate translations, and given that's the status of this particular document, I will not ask him any additional questions on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DB, so when you arrived at the Pribicevac Forward Command Post and you saw Colonel Vukota Vukovic, was there still a tactical group at that location, or was there still a Bratunac Forward Command Post at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date are we talking about now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we're talking about your arrival at the Pribicevac Forward Command Post on the 5th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Bratunac Brigade is concerned, I seem to feel that for the most part at that forward command post, that is to say, in that particular village where the command of one battalion of the Bratunac Brigade was located, that I did see Colonel Blagojevic. I seem to remember that. And on the basis of that, I am able to conclude that for the Krivaja 95 operation, he established a forward command post of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade at Pribicevac in the command of his battalion. He formed the forward command post of his brigade. I assume that that was so because on several occasions I saw him at that command. Whether in that same period Colonel Vukota Vukovic received the assignment to focus his activities on the Skelani Battalion, and I seem to feel that at that time because commanders were frequently replaced in that independent battalion, a corresponding officer did not exist there, and the possibility -- it is possible that Colonel Vukota received an oral order and was designated to direct the operations of that battalion, because I do know that at Pribicevac after combat activity had started, he did not appear. He was constantly with the Skelani Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Colonel -- sorry, did you ever visit Colonel Vukovic's command centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it located in respect of your forward command post communication centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you visited Colonel Vukovic's command centre at Pribicevac. How far away was it from the communications centre of the forward command post of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Vukovic have communications facilities at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had in his office where he stayed one military inductor telephone, which he could reach the command of the 1st Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade which was 100 metres away from him. He could reach their switchboard. That switchboard had connections to certain defence positions integrated in the Pribicevac tactical group. These defence positions were connected in one series so when you called one of the positions, all the telephones on all positions rang, and that was done in order to economise with the field telephone cable. I think that was a pretty secure and reliable communication which was available to Colonel Vukota within his tactical group, and I believe that he must have had another alternative radio communication with at least two or three key positions, in particular, I believe with the Jasenova area. That is my recollection of the organisation of communications for as long as I was with the command of the Pribicevac tactical group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have the ability to communicate with the Bratunac headquarters, the Bratunac command in Bratunac, from his location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have the ability by his radio system to communicate to the Drina Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not through radio communication. He could reach them through radio relay communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you left the forward command post of the Drina Corps on the 11th of July in your communications van, and you went to Bratunac. At the time you left, was Colonel Vukovic's position, his command post that you have just testified about, still in existence when you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these combat operations had developed, together with the entire situation on that part of the front line from the 5th to the 11th, as the army moved on, it was followed by logistics and communications. Colonel Vukota, in view of the fact that he did not come to Pribicevac but instead spent all his time with the Skelani Battalion, and I personally am aware that after the Srebrenica operation was completed, with that unit or a part of those units he took part in the attack -- or rather, demonstrative actions towards Zepa from north to the south. I therefore don't think that he returned to Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, Witness DB. When you left Pribicevac, was Colonel Vukovic's command centre still there on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left on the 11th of July. And speaking in military terms, in view of the development of the situation, I believe that this command centre had no reason to exist whatsoever because Colonel Vukota was far away from it. All the communications were withdrawn by Colonel Blagojevic from that centre towards the area of his attack, so I believe that this communication centre, Colonel Vukota at Pribicevac, ceased to exist on the 11th, that is, on the afternoon of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking according to my information and based on what I know about the development of the military situation because all the units had gone forward, and that communication served nobody at that location any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is not based on your personal observations; is that correct? Did you see the command centre of Colonel Vukovic leave before you left on the night of the 11th? That's the point I'm trying to get to. It was 100 metres away from you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At this command post there was Colonel Blagojevic with his forward command post, and I personally saw Colonel Blagojevic with his signalsman moving and following his army on the directions of attack of his units. And based on that, I conclude that as soon as the army left and Colonel Blagojevic left with his signalsman, there was no longer any need for communications from Pribicevac and no need for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different subject, Witness DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that be a right time now for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It would be fine, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. We will break until 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. Proceed, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the witness could be given the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 784.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before we turn our attention to this particular exhibit, as I understand, the communications centre of the forward command post that you set up at Pribicevac, it was essentially a mobile communications centre with the communications equipment located in a van or a truck. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications centre at the forward command post of the Drina Corps was mobile and was on a truck, that is, on a vehicle, and from that vehicle, using a cable, we could install a telephone at a smaller or greater distance, and radio transmitters could be moved around within a 15-kilometre circle, and we would usually take them out, because those who commanded normally didn't get into a vehicle to issue commands from a vehicle except on rare occasions, when they wanted to use secure communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with your communication, you could communicate with the Main Staff, with the command of the Drina Corps, and with the combat units participating in the operation of Krivaja 95; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, with the proviso that we were able, also through the communications centre of the Drina Corps, to communicate with all the other participants, that is, the entire outside world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could communicate through the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica with the commands of the various brigades within the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have put before you, Witness DB, an exhibit which is the communications system for the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the old JNA communications manual. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to spend a lot of time on this document, Witness, but focusing on your mobile communications centre, you said that you had radio devices. And if you would turn to the section of this plan that deals with the means of communication. In the B/C/S version, Witness, you will see a chart that looks like this. Can you see what I'm holding in my hand, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which page would that be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't tell you, because ... Do you see the chart that deals with the technical details of the radio devices that were available to the JNA? Well, Witness, if it's not in there, then we will -- I'll ask you some questions about the English version of this, which is found on page 9 of the ELMO. I apologise, Witness, if it's not there. Let me proceed, because I don't want to take too much time on this issue. On the ELMO, Witness, there appears a figure that was taken from this manual. It is figure 63 and it is the technical details of some radio devices. Can you tell me: In your mobile communications centre that you established in Pribicevac, what were the names of the radio devices that you had available to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in line 4, where it says RUP-12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And below that there are three additional devices. Did you have any of those devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, do you have anything to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would like to remind the witness that it is on pages 336 and -- 396 and 397 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for his assistance in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beside the RUP-12 at the forward command post, did you have any other radio device that was available to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one technical matter. We had a device called RU-2/2K. It is basically the same as the one in line 4 which I had indicated earlier. It operates in the same frequency range, it has the same number of channels, and two of them can work together, can communicate between them, the only difference being that this device, which is not in this table, can have built into it another device for the protection of speech, for scrambling, and we used that type of device in the command network for communicating to -- commands to orders to subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Witness, am I right the RUP-12 and the RU-2/2K is a tactical communications device that has a rather short range of between 8 and 12 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says in the rules 8 to 12 kilometres; however, deviations are possible here as well. If you read the manual for this device, you will see that the range can be increased with lower frequency -- can be increased with higher frequencies and vice versa, unless there are obstacles on the terrain such as hills, then the range can be greater; and if there are more natural barriers or obstacles, then it can be lower than eight kilometres. And then also when a scrambling device is incorporated into it, then this technical feature makes the device 20 per cent less effective, and its range is decreased accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to radios, did you have a radio telephone device in the mobile communications centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other communications devices did you have in your mobile communications centre besides the two radios that you have described? Can you just give me a list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had telephone devices, that is to say, telephones, field telephones, induction-type telephones of the military kind. We had field telephone switchboards with ten numbers. Furthermore, we had coded teletype machine devices, teletypewriters: the T100, a mechanical type, or the teletype ETL1, an electronic one. We had devices for the protection of written information which is called KZU31, and devices for the protection of oral information, the KZU61 device and KZU63. And with the relay devices, we had a radio relay device which was referred to as RRU1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with the RUP-12, could you communicate outside of the immediate area of the combat theatre? Could you communicate to the headquarters of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the device that you used to communicate with the Drina Corps command from Pribicevac and from the forward command posts that were in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: RRU1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the RRU1 a radio, or does the communication that emanates from a RRU1 between the forward command post and the Drina Corps command consist of a radio beam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the frequency range is between 2 and 300 megahertz. I don't know the exact figure, but basically they are beamed radio waves. They are beamed. They are radio waves that are beamed. And we had this type of communication with the help of a stationary junction, Veliki Zep, and it is from that area, both from Srebrenica and from Zepa, that radio relay line was not a direct one, but it was beamed via the radio relay junction at Veliki Zep which is close to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the signal would go from you to Veliki Zep, be relayed from Veliki Zep to the command at Vlasenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also had a teleprinter. You described the names of those teleprinters -- actually, before I -- let me withdraw that question, and let me show the witness one additional exhibit before I get to teleprinters. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 826, and if I could have the witness examine this communications device. Witness DB, in this Prosecutor's exhibit there is a man with a black uniform, and he has a radio communication device on his back. Can you identify that radio device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I can't see the other side well enough where we attached the device to the protection device, but according to what I can see and the black part, it could be the RU-2/2K device. But at all events, if the device has not been attached, which I can't see on the other side, it is one of the two devices that we talked about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, let's turn to teleprinters. Can you tell us very, very briefly about a teleprinter and how it communicates from point A, the forward command post, to the command at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer in the technical sense would be a little more complex. I'll try and make it as clear as possible, but please bear with me. In order to have teleprinter communication from the forward command posts, we had that with the use of just one channel which we established with the radio relay device, the RRU1 device. That means that while the teleprinter was working, and either receiving or sending out messages, during that period of time you can't talk to anybody else. The teleprinter is a device which has as its -- which has a print board, and its purpose is to type out certain information or a message, and that information uses a paper tape or sheet of paper coded for each letter. It is 17 and a half millimetres wide, so it is still an open text. Later on, that tape is introduced into a device for the coding of that written information, encryption, and a communication is established with the participant to whom we wish to send out that information, a button is pressed, the start button is depressed, and the tape then passes through and is locked or coded at the same time and goes to the other side. The other side, the other party, takes up the tape, introduces it into the device which has the same lock to unlock it or decode it or decipher it, and then we get the printed text. It is the key which unlocks this, and this is done on a page of 10 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have one teleprinter in your van, or did you have more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have one teleprinter device in your mobile communications van when you were in Pribicevac and Zepa, or did you have more than one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on logic, we probably had at least two teleprinters, because if one were out of order, we were able to send out messages with the other. So that was logical. That was the logical back-up system that we had when we were on assignments of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Pribicevac and Zepa, did you have breakdowns with those teleprinters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those teleprinters function exclusively on 220 volts, whereas the other devices can function using 12 volts, a 12-volt system. So there were breakdowns from time to time, but they were not as frequent and not as important to upset control and command, because I know that I was not criticised for my communications system, although breakdowns could occur from time to time, either on our side or at the stationary junction or at the ultimate destination, the communications centre of the Drina Corps. So the number of -- the human factor is multiplied by three there, because if you have this triple link, there are two ends and one intermediary point, and therefore it is possible that there are reasons for a breakdown of a technical nature or human error. But as I say, I don't think that there were any major upsets in the system of communications, and I want to repeat that here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you a portion of General Krstic's testimony that was taken on the 31st of October, and I'm referring to page 6673 of the transcript, lines 5 through 19 of the English version. This was a question asked by my colleague, Mr. McCloskey: "Q. While you were in the forward command post, did you have the capability of receiving orders like this in a secure manner?" And this was a teletype document. "A. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't describe to you how it worked. There is a communications centre with officers and soldiers of the communications department, work led by their commander, the communications commander, battalion -- I'm sorry -- battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the VRS at that time had the capability of teletyping an order like this, that is, typing in the information and sending it via teletype in encrypted teletype?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, but there were some problems, and the teletype very often didn't work, and there was no electricity for the signals and communications to function properly. There was a breakdown in the system very often." Apparently General Krstic, from his point of view, has a slightly different viewpoint of the workings of the teletypes. Do you care to comment on this testimony provided by General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very often my superior commanders and their assistants were warned by me. I warned them, cautioned them, and asked that longer reports with a number of pages of -- typed pages, if possible, to send them by courier link, because if you want to hand over just two pages of a typed-out text, then via the teleprinter and via the radio relay waves, this takes five minutes. There are orders, certain orders, which are longer than two typed-out pages, and then there is the possibility that just one interference signal, which lasts for just one second, breaks down the whole system of reception, and then you have to ask the telegramme repeated in its entirety. Or the opposite side, quite simply, as this message is long-winded and takes a long time, succeeds in decoding it, and that is why teleprinters are exclusively intended for the transmission of important, urgent, and short messages. And I'm speaking on the basis of my recollections, and I have no reason at this point in time to say how good my work was at that time, but as far as I remember, those interruptions were not very frequent for them to be -- to upset the control and command system in its global sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about couriers for a minute. At both the Pribicevac Forward Command Post and the forward command post that you used in Zepa, did you use couriers to communicate with the Bratunac Brigade headquarters -- I'm sorry -- the Drina Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time I spent at the forward command post of Pribicevac, in view of the fact that it is at quite a distance from the command of the Bratunac Brigade itself and a good deal greater from the command of the Drina Corps, a good deal further off from the Drina Corps, it would not be a rational link to use a courier, and I'm quite sure that as far as the communication centre, we did not organise it, and I can only assume that nobody else in the capacity of a courier from the forward command post at Pribicevac did not carry any written messages, or oral ones, for that matter. By moving to the forward command post at Krivace, as that was very close to the command of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska -- I don't know exactly how close, but it was four, five, or six kilometres, thereabouts, and some 30-odd kilometres from the command of the Drina Corps -- I, as a communications man, did not plan to have any courier communication, but it is quite possible that certain messages in written form, via some other individuals, drivers, for example, from the staff command, or by some transport coming back from the logistics base, might have carried information of this kind. But we adhered to the rule that the safest communication was a courier communication, in fact, and that couriers should be used whenever possible, whenever it was indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm a little confused by your answer. Did you or did you not use courier communication from the Pribicevac Forward Command Post and the Zepa Forward Command Post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this. In order to plan and organise a courier link, courier links are planned by the chief of communications, and I know that as a signalsman, we did not have a permanent courier link, courier communication. But in wartime, when you had to fend for yourself and do what you could, there was a possibility that certain written messages could be transmitted by other means, by people who actually took on the role of courier and acted as couriers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when courier messages were received at the forward command post, were they logged, were they entered, or were the courier packages given directly to the person who was the intended recipient of those courier parcels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations, and we had an organised system of courier communications of the Drina Corps for certain messages which were not urgent and important, couriers bringing the message or messages would go to the dispatch unit and the dispatcher would sign for the reception of certain messages, sign that he had received them. So according to the rules, every message or document going by courier must have -- must be registered in the dispatch centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to change our subject again, and if I could have the witness provided with Exhibit 750.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the B/C/S version portion that I would like you to take a look at is found on page 37 of the document. And this is a document that is an analysis of the combat readiness and the activities of the army of the Republika Srpska in 1992. This was prepared by the army of the Republika Srpska, and the date on this is April of 1993. Now, the section that I'd like to refer you to is the section that deals with electronic reconnaissance and counter-electronic operations units. And in this analysis of the activities of the army, this section deals with the analysis of that particular activity. Now, first of all, Witness, before you read much of this, let me ask you: Did the electronic reconnaissance operations, the intercepting groups that were in the VRS, fall under the purview of the intelligence department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had, for example, a unit that ranked with the radio reconnaissance platoon, which in the professional sense was subordinated to the intelligence department, just as the Communications Battalion in the professional sense was subordinated to the communications chief, chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read to you the -- actually, Witness, this might be of better assistance to you. If you take my copy, I've highlighted the portions that I'm going to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we are on page 41, I'm sorry, Mr. Usher, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm referring to the first highlighted area, and I will read this to you, "On account --" starting in the second sentence of the second paragraph. "On account of the above and a number of other difficulties, it was decided to form radio reconnaissance platoons (RIVs) in the corps to engage in electronic reconnaissance, interception, interference, misinforming and deceiving the enemy using his system of communications. By the end of 1992, the platoons had been trained to intercept, identify, and present indicators of the offensive intentions of the enemy vis-a-vis RS and the VRS, and to gather information about the enemy (formation strength, disposition, and intentions) for the needs of the corps and the Main Staff of the VRS." And the fourth paragraph I've highlighted an area for you, Witness, it's the first -- it reads as follows: "To the extent permitted by the technical possibilities, the RIVs," which are the radio reconnaissance platoons, "organise their work in radio reconnaissance groups so that the six corps, the air force, the anti-aircraft defence, as well as the VRS Main Staff receive intelligence from 16 radio reconnaissance groups." The following paragraph reads, the first part of it, "The total number of RIV," that's radio reconnaissance platoon, "personnel is 130 soldiers and officers. Through its work so far, this formation has provided the command structures with about 70 per cent of all the intelligence data gathered. The importance of this activity is enormous." Now, reading on to the following paragraph, I'd like to read a portion of this. "The EI system," and EI is electronic reconnaissance, "that was made for successful reconnaissance and interception of enemy tactical and operational strategic radio and radio relay communications, due to the size of the theatre of war, these interception groups collected data at all levels of the enemy's system. This made it possible to deploy radio interception groups, RIGs, in the immediate vicinity of the front line of defence, exclusively at points dominating the enemy's battle positions." Now, my first question -- let me read one more portion of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is found on page 42, Mr. Usher, toward the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "All 16 RIGs were connected to corps intelligence and security bodies by one or more communication channels as well as to the tactical and operational group in whose zone they worked." The next paragraph, "The processing and distribution of intelligence obtained by EI is carried out by intelligence squads in the corps and the air force and the anti-aircraft defence, fully applying crypto-protection measures." The next paragraph, "The available technical, personnel, and material potentials make possible the successful simultaneous surveillance of between 50 and 60 radio channels at all levels of over 600 linked up channels. We cannot listen to about 100 channels because of crypto-protection measures applied or technical inadequacy of our equipment." Now, this is in 1992, Witness, and one can see from this description provided by the VRS of its activities in 1992, that they had collected -- that these groups were responsible for collecting 70 per cent of the intelligence gathered by the VRS, and it appears from this description that this operation and procedure was successful and relied upon by the Main Staff and the corps. Do you agree with me with this, or do you have any comment that you'd like to make in light of what I've read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an analysis of combat readiness of the army of Republika Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srpska in 1992, and this portion on units in all this material was probably compiled and drafted and sent to the chief for electronic surveillance and counter-electronic operations, and he probably did so on the basis of the information he had at his particular level. And I don't have any particular comments to make in this regard and in view of what is written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the data that was collected by the radio reconnaissance groups went to a particular entity within the sphere of operation of the intelligence operation of the corps staff, specifically, the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon in the Drina Corps; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps had a radio reconnaissance platoon. I don't know whether it was called the 4th because there was only one, but it had a radio reconnaissance platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, in the Prosecutor's Exhibit 28, one can see that the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon is found in the box dealing with the intelligence section, the chief of which is Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Kosoric, and the assistant in entity is Major Pavle Golic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in the army throughout the war. Would the radio -- I see my colleague is on his feet, so I will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know, it remained unclear whether this was a question of Mr. Harmon, this reference to the two officers who were representatives of this radio reconnaissance unit, or it is a claim of Mr. Harmon's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think Mr. Harmon is the best to answer this. I was going to ask him something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I will answer the concerns of my colleague. I was merely pointing out the location in the structure where the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon is. It falls within the ambit of the intelligence section whose head is Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Golic is the assistant, or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask this witness if he knows because we had testimony on this point previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know Lieutenant -- I'm sorry, Major Pavle Golic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his role in the intelligence section?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the intelligence sector, but I don't know what his role was. But I wish to say that the two officers you mentioned were not commanders of the radio reconnaissance platoon. The commander of that platoon was the captain, and this radio reconnaissance platoon, professionally speaking was subordinated -- responsible to the intelligence organ and provided information to the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness DB, the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon had its groups within the Drina Corps area of responsibility, it collected radio intercept information, and it forwarded that information to the intelligence section, did it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the 4th Radio Reconnaissance Platoon that operated in the Drina Corps area of operation, in other core areas there were similar radio reconnaissance platoons that collected intercept operation -- information, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they didn't collect the information merely to collect the information; they collected the information in order to share it with the relevant branches that may potentially be affected by that sensitive information, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if another corps area was intercepting information that related to, for example, the operations of the Drina Corps, that sensitive information would be sent down to the Drina Corps, to the intelligence section of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know Colonel Kosoric, Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what his relationship was to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the military relationship, or some other relationship?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In some other relationship.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean private, personal, family relationship?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are related.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric is General Krstic's brother-in-law, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric during the Zepa -- I'm sorry, during the Srebrenica operation was at the forward command post throughout the period of time that the Srebrenica operation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric was there the whole time, but my -- from my recollection, he had greater freedom to leave that forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he left from time to time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, meaning that he didn't spend as much time as I did on the forward command post every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Zepa, Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Kosoric was likewise at the forward command posts that were established at the Zepa operation, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was at the forward command post for the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he remain in Zepa throughout the period of time of that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that, for instance, he would not spend as much time as I would during the day at the forward command post -- at the command post. His job was not to stay at the command post all the time as I was supposed to, and that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric continued to have obligations as the chief of intelligence for the Drina Corps while he was at both of those command posts, forward command post, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it fair to assume, Witness DB, that he was informed of intelligence developments while he was out of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the command in Vlasenica, when he was outside the command in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was outside of the command in Vlasenica, he continued with his responsibilities as the chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps, and I assume, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, that he continued to be informed by his subordinates of relevant and important intelligence information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if those were his orders to them, and if he insisted to be kept informed of all the developments while he was outside the command of the corps, or to give -- to keep informed his deputy, or if such information was particularly important, important enough to be given personally to the commander, then they would have done so. If he had ordered them to send him information wherever he was at the time, then they would have done so. But perhaps they might have done so and forwarded the information to his deputy at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Riad, we're going to stop at 3.00, are we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you have any other suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have four exhibits I'd like to go through with this witness and I will try to be as quick as I can with them, or we can adjourn now and I can review them tomorrow morning with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I prefer that last option, because I prefer that we proceed in some kind of coherent series of questions. So I don't want to stop you in the middle of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It won't be stopping me in the middle, but I would not want to be stopped with two documents into this and lose the thread of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So how much time do you need now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would say I need ten minutes with these exhibits and we would be required to go over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll give you 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I appreciate it, Judge, and I will accept. If I could have four exhibits given to the usher. They are exhibits 364/12. And actually, Judge, I see this is a document that is under seal and will require a private session, so my 12 minutes may not be enough time getting in and out of private session. So perhaps if we can adjourn now, I can resolve this matter in 12 minutes or 15 minutes tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We will be having enough time tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How much time do you expect to be in need of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think I have not progressed as quickly as I had hoped and I may need the complete day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Complete day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We'll give you a complete day. Thank you. I think we'll adjourn till tomorrow morning, 9.20. I hope we can have good news about General Krstic's health, and I request that Mr. Petrusic can inform us tomorrow morning. We are adjourned
